{{technical|date=January 2026}}
{{short description|Statistical test for goodness-of-fit}}

The '''Berk-Jones test''' (or '''BJ test''') refers to a class of non-parametric [[goodness-of-fit]] statistical tests used to determine whether a set of observed data follow a specific [[probability distribution]]. Introduced by [[Robert H. Berk]] and [[Douglas H. Jones]] in 1979, the test is specifically designed to be more powerful than the [[Kolmogorov-Smirnov test]] in the tails of the distribution.<ref name="BerkJones1979">{{cite journal |last1=Berk |first1=R. H. |last2=Jones |first2=D. H. |date=1979 |title=Relatively Optimal Combinations of Test Statistics |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/4615706.pdf |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Statistics |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=33–36}}</ref>

==Background==
In [[statistical hypothesis testing]], a goodness-of-fit test compares an [[empirical distribution function]] (EDF) to a theoretical [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF). While the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is arguably the most well-known method, it is often criticized for its lack of sensitivity to deviations occurring at the extremes (tails) of the distribution.

The Berk-Jones test addresses this shortcoming by adopting a "pointwise" maximum [[likelihood ratio]] approach. It still belongs to the family of supremum-type statistics but also incorporates information-theoretic properties, specifically the [[Kullback-Leibler divergence]].

==Mathematical formulation==
Let <math>X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n</math> be [[independent and identically distributed]] (i.i.d.) random variables with an empirical distribution function <math>\mathbb{F}_n(x)</math>. We wish to test the [[null hypothesis]] <math>H_0: F = F_0</math>.

The Berk-Jones statistic <math>R_n</math> is defined as:
:<math>R_n = \sup_{x} K(\mathbb{F}_n(x), F_0(x))</math>
where <math>K(p,q)</math> is the binary Kullback-Leibler divergence (or [[relative entropy]]), defined as:
:<math>K(p,q) = p \log \left(\frac{p}{q}\right) + \left(1-p\right)\log\left(\frac{1-p}{1-q}\right)</math>
The statistic can also be expressed in terms of the [[order statistic]]s <math>X_{(1)} < X_{(2)} < \cdots <X_{(n)}</math>. For a fixed <math>x</math>, <math>n\,\mathbb{F}_n(x)</math> follows a [[Binomial distribution]] <math>\text{Bin}(n, F_0(x))</math>. The BJ statistic effectively finds the <math>x</math> that maximizes the likelihood ratio for testing the success probability of this binomial.<ref name="Wellner2007">{{cite journal |last1=Wellner |first1=J. A. |last2=Jager |first2=L. |date=2007 |title=Goodness-of-fit tests via Phi-divergences |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-35/issue-5/Goodness-of-fit-tests-via-phi-divergences/10.1214/0009053607000000244.full |journal=The Annals of Statistics |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=2018–2053}}</ref>

==Relationship with Tukey's Higher Criticism statistic==
The Berk-Jones test is closely related to the [[Higher Criticism statistic]] (HC), originally suggested by [[John Tukey]] in 1976 and further developed in 2004 by [[David Donoho]] and [[Jianshun Jin]]. Both tests are used for sparse [[signal detection]].

While the BJ test is based on the likelihood ratio, the HC statistic is based on a standardized distance (essentially a [[Z score]] approach):
:<math>\text{HC}_n = \sup_{x} \frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\mathbb{F}_n(x) - F_0(x)\right)}{\sqrt{F_0(x)\left(1 - F_0(x)\right)}}</math>
Asymptotically (as <math>n</math> approaches infinity), the BJ test and HC are equivalent in their ability to detect sparse mixtures. Specifically, they both belong to the [[Rényi family]] of statistics. However, the BJ test is over viewed as the "information-theoretic version" of HC. When applying a [[Taylor expansion]] to the Kullback-Leibler divergence <math>K(p,q)</math> around <math>p=q</math>, the first non-vanishing term in the expansion is proportional to the square of the HC statistic:<ref name="Donoho2004">{{cite journal |last1=Donoho |first1=D. |last2=Jin |first2=J. |date=2004 |title=Higher Criticism for detecting sparse heterogeneous mixtures |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-32/issue-3/Higher-criticism-for-detecting-sparse-heterogeneous-mixtures/10.1214/009053604000000265.full |journal=The Annals of Statistics |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=962–994}}</ref>
:<math>K(p,q) \approxeq \frac{(p-q)^2}{2q(1-q)}</math>
This shows that the Higher Criticism statistic is essentially a local [[quadratic approximation]] of the Berk-Jones statistic.

In high-dimensional settings where the signal is "rare and weak," both tests have the same [[detection boundary]] (the point at which it becomes mathematically possible to distinguish signal from noise). However, the BJ test is often preferred in finite samples of the <math>[0,1]</math> interval more naturally than the <math>Z</math>-score denominator in HC.

==Comparison of power==
The effectiveness of the Berk-Jones test compared with other methods depends heavily on the nature of the deviation from the null hypothesis.

{| class="wikitable"
! Test Method !! Sensitivity Focus !! Best Use Case
|-
| '''Kolmogorov–Smirnov''' || Median / Center || General deviations in the bulk of the data.
|-
| '''Anderson–Darling''' || Weighted Tails || Moderate tail sensitivity; common in engineering.
|-
| '''Berk–Jones''' || Extreme Tails || Sparse signals; likelihood-ratio based optimality.
|-
| '''Higher Criticism''' || Extreme Tails || Sparse signals; <math>Z</math>-score based optimality.
|}

==Applications==
The Berk-Jones test is widely used in:
* [[Genomics]]: for identifying differentially expressed genes where only a small fraction of genes are expected to show a signal.
* [[Signal detection]]: for detecting weak, sparse signals against a background of noise.
* [[Meta-analysis]]: for combining p-values from multiple independent studies to detect a global effect.
